t.1.143.1: Rākṣasas remember an enmity, resorting to bewildering illusion. Hiḍimbā, go you along the path that your brother has taken.
t.1.143.2: Even though you are angry, O tiger among men, O Bhīma, do not kill a woman! Guard dharma, O Pāṇḍava, which is greater than the protection of the body.
t.1.143.3: You have slain that mighty one who came upon us intent on killing; what can the sister of that rākṣasa, enraged, do to us?
t.1.143.4: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Hiḍimbā, having saluted Kuntī with joined palms, spoke these words to her and to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
t.1.143.5: Noble lady, you know the suffering that women in this world feel, born of the bodiless god of love; that very suffering has now come upon me, caused by Bhīmasena, O fair one.
t.1.143.7: For, having abandoned my friends, my own dharma and my own kin, I have chosen this tiger among men, your son, as my husband, O fair lady.
t.1.143.6: That supreme sorrow was endured by me as I waited for the right time; that time has now arrived, and it will surely be for my happiness.
t.1.143.9: Whether you think of me as a foolish woman, or as one devoted and following you, O illustrious lady, unite me with this son of yours as my husband.
t.1.143.8: Though I spoke thus, glorious lady, I was then rejected in this matter both by this chosen husband of mine and by you as well.
t.1.143.11: For whenever I am called to mind, I shall always carry you all wherever you wish; in danger and in difficult straits I shall bring you, bulls among men, safely across.
t.1.143.10: Taking him, who has the form of a god, let me go wherever I please, and I will surely come back again; put your trust in me, O fair lady.
t.1.143.13: In crossing over a calamity, by whatever means one can keep one's life, all that must be done, and done with care, by one who follows dharma.
t.1.143.12: I will carry you on my back, you who desire swift passage; grant me your favor, so that Bhīmasena may take me as his own.
t.1.143.14: He who upholds dharma in times of calamity is the best, O knower of dharma; for it is a misfortune befalling dharma itself that is called a calamity by those devoted to dharma.
t.1.143.16: It is just as you have said, Hiḍimbā; there is no doubt about this. But you must abide by dharma, O slender-waisted one, as I shall tell you.
t.1.143.15: Merit sustains the life-breaths; merit is called the giver of life. By whatever means one may practise dharma, no blame is found in it.
t.1.143.17: Once Bhīmasena has bathed, performed his daily rites and had the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony performed, good lady, you may attend upon him until the setting of the sun.
t.1.143.18: By day, swift as thought, sport with him as you please; but this Bhīmasena must always be brought back by you at night.
t.1.143.19: Then the Rākṣasī Hiḍimbā, promising, "So be it," took up Bhīmasena and thereupon rose up into the sky.
t.1.143.20: On lovely mountain peaks and in the sanctuaries of the gods, places resounding with the cries of beasts and birds and delightful at all times,
t.1.143.22: And likewise in forest fastnesses, on mountain slopes covered with flowering trees, and in lovely lakes filled with lotuses and water lilies.
t.1.143.23: On the islands in rivers, on sands glittering like beryl, in waters with fine fords and woods along their banks, and likewise in mountain streams.
t.1.143.21: Assuming a supremely beautiful form and adorned with every ornament, she, chatting most sweetly, delighted the Pāṇḍava.
t.1.143.24: In the regions of the ocean strewn with gems and gold, in delightful towns, and in forests of great śāla trees,
t.1.143.25: In the holy forests of the gods and on the slopes of mountains, in the dwellings of the Guhyakas and in the retreats of ascetics.
t.1.143.27: Then, delighting Bhīma here and there, the rākṣasī, swift as thought, bore to Bhīmasena a son of great strength.
t.1.143.26: Amid the fruits and flowers of every season, and by the lakes of Mānasa, she, bearing a supremely beautiful form, delighted the Pāṇḍava.
t.1.143.28: One with misshapen eyes, a huge mouth and ears pointed like spikes, terrifying and dreadful in form, with deep copper-red lips, sharp fangs, and mighty strength.
t.1.143.29: Him, a great archer of great valor and great spirit, mighty-armed, of great speed and huge body, a master of great magic, a tamer of foes.
t.1.143.31: Though still a child, O lord of the people, he had already reached youth among humans, and the mighty hero attained supreme pre-eminence in all weapons.
t.1.143.30: She bore a son, superhuman though born of a human, of fearsome speed and mighty strength, who far surpassed the other piśācas and surpassed humans as well.
t.1.143.32: For rākṣasīs conceive at once and give birth at once, and they become shape-shifters, taking on many forms at will.
t.1.143.33: Then the bald one, a great archer, bowed down and clasped the feet of his father and his mother, and the two of them gave him his name.
t.1.143.35: And that Ghaṭotkaca was devoted to those Pāṇḍavas, and he became ever dear to them, as one of their very own selves.
t.1.143.34: "He is hairless, gleaming like a pot," he said to the mother; and because of that his name became Ghaṭotkaca.
t.1.143.36: Then Hiḍimbā said to him, "The agreed term of our living together has come to an end," and, having made an agreement, she went her own way.
t.1.143.38: For he was created by the great-souled Maghavat, for the sake of the spear, to bring about the destruction of the great-souled Karṇa of unrivalled valour.
t.1.143.37: "When there is work to be done, I shall come to you," said Ghaṭotkaca, and, taking leave of his fathers, that best of Rākṣasas set out toward the northern direction.
